next-season-styles

Three garments a forecast chose, and the pictures made from them.

What to look at first

What the model predicted. From two years of H&M sales it ranked about 2,000 clothing styles by how hard each would sell, per product on sale, over the 13 weeks after 21 September 2020, and its top picks, after a human editorial rule that removed intimates and required three different colours, were a black jersey T-shirt, a beige knit sweater and a red dress.

What was generated from it. For each style, an image generator was given real H&M product photos of that style as a guide and asked for a new garment; the three pictures above are the best of eight tries each (two rounds of four).

How to judge whether it worked. Two questions: does each picture look like a believable, new product of its style (section 1: 1 of 3 passed every automatic check, and none of the three shows the design change that was asked for), and does the forecast beat guessing and simple rules of thumb (section 3, where it names the right neighbourhood about 72% of the time against 0.4% for chance)?

The three concepts

Each block: the picture, what it shows, and four checks. Every number is followed by what it means. The measures behind the checks are explained once, after the third concept.

Black jersey T-shirt

Did not pass one check: its closest reference photo is a shade closer than any two real products of this style are.

Why this failure is meaningful, not noise

The limit was built from real T-shirts (how close do two genuine H&M black tees get to each other?) and tested on a control: an exact copy of a reference photo fails it in every style. It flagged this concept, and a person comparing the picture with the design brief reached the same conclusion from a different direction: the brief asked for charcoal stitching and a cropped, dropped-shoulder cut, and neither is visible. This is a plain black tee like the ones already on sale.

Two independent checks agreeing is the evidence that the check works. We did not loosen the limit to make this pass. What it does not show is a copy of one particular photo: next to its closest reference photo the concept has a different cut. It is a basic that adds nothing over what exists, which is exactly the kind of concept the check exists to flag.

The 6 real H&M photos it was guided by

What the measures mean

CLIP and DINOv2 are two pretrained image models that turn a picture into numbers so pictures can be compared; 1.0 means identical, and real product photos of one style score around 0.85 to 0.97 because they share the same studio setup. CLIP compares overall look; DINOv2 compares shape and texture. A check passes only if both measures pass.

A limit here is the 90th percentile of the same measure taken between real H&M products of that style: 9 in 10 real pairs fall below it. With only 4 to 6 real reference photos per style these limits are rough.

How each concept traces back to its predicted style

Read each row left to right: what the model forecast, why, which photos guided the picture, what the design brief asked for, and what the picture actually shows.

Black jersey T-shirt

  1. Forecast

    Predicted 33.8 units per product on sale per week for the 13 weeks after 21 Sep 2020; an established seller (top of the 'incumbent' list).

    "Intensity" means units sold per product on sale, so a style is not ranked highly just for having many products.

  2. Why the model liked it

    Biggest influences, in order: last week's sales level for this style, then how many products of this style are on sale, then the time-of-year pattern.

    These come from an explanation method called SHAP, which shows which inputs pushed this forecast up or down. Persistence (lag_1) dominates over seasonal.

  3. Guided by

    The first photo is the one the generator actually copies structure from.

    • oversized cropped boxy fit, wide sleeves
    • white contrast neckband and sleeve bands

    These were instructions to the generator, not results.

    Short-sleeve ribbed tee, grey body with black sleeves and neckband.

    Described by looking at the image. None of the requested changes is visible in these three pictures; the human check for each is in section 1.

Does the model actually predict?

The model is scored on 12 past dates: at each, it trains only on earlier data and forecasts the next 13 weeks, and we compare with what happened.

Hit@3 in top 20 = 0.722
When the model names its three best styles, they land in the true top 20 (of about 3,000 styles) about 72% of the time. Random guessing scores 0.4%. This is the headline number.
Hit@3 in top 10 = 0.500
The same, against the true top 10: 50% for the model, 0.3% for guessing.
Precision@3 = 0.056
How often the three named styles are exactly the true top three, in any order: 5.6%, guessing 0.1%. This is low for every method because the true #3 and #4 styles differ by about half a percent of sales, so the model finds the right neighbourhood, not the exact order.
NDCG@10 = 0.900
Scores the model's top 10 by how much real demand they carry (1.0 is perfect). Even random picks score 0.40, because most styles sell similar amounts, so read 0.90 against 0.40.
Spearman = 0.803
How closely the model's full ranking of all styles matches the true ranking: 1 is identical, 0 is unrelated. Guessing gives 0.000.

Each cell is the average over 12 test dates the model never saw, with a 95% interval in brackets. "Model minus this" is the model advantage over that method on the same dates; an interval entirely above zero means the advantage is reliable.

How do we know the forecast isn't cheating?

We scrambled which sales figure belongs to which style, retrained the same model three times, and scored it on the real answers. It collapsed to chance: 0 hits in 108 picks (Hit@3 in top 20 = 0.000, guessing scores 0.004). Run through the same code without scrambling, it reproduces 0.722. If information from the future had leaked into the inputs, the scrambled model could not have fallen to chance.

A spot-check you can see

Both panels share one vertical scale. The dark line is what each style actually sold per product on sale over the last 26 weeks of data; the blue bar is the model's forecast for the following 13 weeks (unobserved; the data ends 21 Sep 2020). The top-ranked style sells several times more than one ranked 1,500th, and the forecast reflects that. It also shows the forecast pulling back from a late-summer spike rather than extrapolating it.

For summer, the model was re-run as of 1 June 2020 (using only earlier data). It ranked swimwear bottoms 1 of 2,763 and predicted 93.1 units per product per week for June to August; the realised figure was 50.0, so the model got the ranking right but overshot the level by about 86%.

The tables show each season's historical average weekly intensity among styles that pass the three sanity guards (enough products on sale, no heavy discounting, sold in most recent weeks).

The summer concept: four tries, one chosen

Chosen by eye. Two of the other three passed the automatic similarity checks anyway: one drifted to a grey pinstripe, one has straps sewn onto a bottom.

Fits in with real products of its stylePassed

CLIP 0.945 (limit 0.982), DINOv2 0.917 (limit 0.967).

Not a copy of any single photoPassed

Closest reference photo: CLIP 0.958 (limit 0.986), DINOv2 0.942 (limit 0.989). An exact copy fails this test.

Matches the style's visible attributesPassed

three readings; the middle value is 0.562 counting only the visible attributes (product type and colour) against a pass mark of 0.513, and 0.375 if the catalogue label "Other structure" is also counted. Both figures are shown; the visible-only one is the rule.

"Other structure" is an internal catalogue catch-all, not a pattern a viewer can name, so it is excluded from the check (the same fix as for "Jersey Basic" earlier); the image reader described the picture correctly as "solid, ribbed". The pass is narrow: 0.049 over the mark, well inside the ±0.21 noise between readings. The reference photos were screened by eye because the automatic framing check was out of free quota.

What we could not verify

  • Whether the pictures would sell. The forecast is about styles; the pictures are new designs no customer has seen. Nothing here tests demand for the pictures themselves.
  • Demand, as opposed to sales. Everything derives from what was stocked and sold, not what customers wanted. No inventory data was available; a stock-out check finds a lower bound of 3.76% of style-weeks with a stock-out signature.
  • The AI image reader is noisy and there is only one. The same picture scored differently by up to ±0.21 across sessions, every fidelity score comes from one model, and a second reader was unavailable (free-tier limits). The sweater's "melange" scored 0 although the flecking is visible: that is a genuine reader error and stays in its score.
  • Automatic checks miss broken garments. In an earlier exploration (red underwear, since retired as a final concept because intimates are excluded by an editorial rule) three of the four regenerated candidates were visibly malformed (a cut-out defect, sheer mesh, an unrecognisable folded object) and still passed every automatic check. A human check is required.
  • None of the three concepts shows its briefed design change. After two rounds of four tries per style, the generator kept the structure of the first reference photo and ignored the requested changes (cropped fit and white bands, funnel neck and brown rib, puff sleeves and belt). The T-shirt is a grey-bodied colour-block tee the brief never asked for, the sweater is a generic beige V-neck and the dress drifted from red to coral-pink. Passing the automatic checks did not make them new designs.
  • The limits behind the checks are rough. Each rests on only 4 to 6 real reference photos per style.
  • The exact top three. The model finds the right neighbourhood (72% in the true top 20) but not the exact order (5.6% exactly right), because the leaders are nearly tied.
  • COVID. The test window includes spring 2020; results are reported pooled and split, but the splits are too small to be more than directional.
  • The summer concept's reference photos were screened by eye, because the automatic framing judges were out of free quota that day.
